title: Queen Helena
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: Hyman writes: This precious woman, although she did not come from the loins of Judah, merited eternal remembrance for praise and glory.

Hyman relates that she was the wife of King Hadiv, and her two sons, Monobuz [מונבוז] and Zotos, accepted the religion of Israel through a certain Hebrew merchant named Hananiah the Babylonian, who came to them and taught them the Torah of Israel; afterward, through Eleazar from the Galilee, they circumcised themselves, and their mother agreed to this. Hyman cites [Antiquities of the Jews 20.34–48](https://lexundria.com/j_aj/20.34-48/wst) for this account; it is mentioned briefly in [Bereshit Rabbah ch. 46, section 10](https://www.sefaria.org/Bereshit_Rabbah.46.10). And Helena, their mother, converted and cleaved with all her heart to the Torah of Israel. In [Nazir ch. 3, mishnah 6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Nazir.3.6), an incident is told of Helena the queen, whose son went to war, and she said: If my son comes back from the war in peace, I will be a nazirite for seven years. At the end of seven years she went up to the Land, and Beit Hillel ruled that she should be a nazirite for another seven years. And in [Yoma ch. 3, mishnah 10](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Yoma.3.10): King Monobaz made all the handles of the vessels of Yom Kippur of gold; Helena his mother made a golden candelabrum over the entrance of the Sanctuary, and she also made a golden tablet on which the passage of the sotah was written. And in [Sukkah 2b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sukkah.2b.15): An incident occurred with Helena the queen in Lod, whose sukkah was higher than twenty cubits, and she had seven sons, and all her deeds she did only on the advice of the Sages.

Hyman relates, citing [Antiquities of the Jews 20.51](https://lexundria.com/j_aj/20.51/wst), that in her days there was a great famine in the land of Judah, and then she opened her treasuries and saved the people from hunger.
Hyman cites Bava Batra 11b for the corresponding account at [11a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.11a.3-4), in which King Monobaz freely distributed his treasures and the treasures of his fathers in years of drought; and Hyman explains that this is because her son was then king, therefore the great acts of charity were attributed to his name.

Hyman’s opening genealogy and conversion narrative remains his synthesis attributed to Antiquities of the Jews; that work has not been freshly collated here. The entire named Midrash Rabbah—TE Bereshit Rabbah 46:10 paragraph has Monobaz and Zavatos as sons of King Talmai and their mother’s intervention, without naming Helena, Hananiah or Eleazar. It does not verify the whole synthesis or reconcile Talmai with the supplied Hadiv, or Zavatos with Zotos. The whole Torat Emet Mishnah Nazir 3:6 confirms the seven-plus-seven-year instruction; its further twenty-one/fourteen-year discussion is not added. The whole Torat Emet Mishnah Yoma 3:10 confirms Monobaz’s golden handles and Helena his mother’s candelabrum and tablet. The whole Davidson Sukkah 2b paragraph confirms Lod, more than twenty cubits, seven sons and action on the Sages’ advice. All twelve Davidson paragraphs of Bava Batra 11b were read and do not contain the treasure-distribution episode; the two whole paragraphs at 11a do contain Monobaz distributing his own and his fathers’ treasures in drought years. This is a separate positive comparison, without changing the supplied יא: or the literal English 11b. The earlier note’s 11b statement concerns transcription of the supplied locator, not proof that the episode occurs there. Hyman’s explanation attributing the charity to her son because he was then king remains his interpretation. The earlier note’s reference to a king named בנה is retained verbatim as historical editorial uncertainty; the present rendering reads “her son.” Monobuz [מונבוז], later Monobaz [מונבז], Zotos, Hadiv, the supplied עור and יו״הכפ and all questions remain unchanged. These digital comparisons establish no canonical identities, genealogy, chronology, printed-source corrections or hold clearance.

Josephus (Antiquities 20.2.1–4, Whiston translation) calls Helena’s husband and brother Monobazus, also named Bazeus, king of Adiabene. He names their sons as the elder Monobazus and Izates. In his account the merchant Ananias teaches Izates, another Jewish teacher instructs Helena, and Helena and Ananias initially urge Izates to refrain from circumcision. Eleazar from Galilee subsequently persuades Izates, and a surgeon performs it. Hyman’s printed Hadiv, Zotos, two-son account and report of Helena’s consent are retained as his account. The distinct names and actors in Bereshit Rabbah 46:10 remain a separate comparison.

Josephus (Antiquities 20.2.5 and 20.5.2) describes Helena purchasing and distributing food during the famine. He also records separate aid from her son Izates, who was then king. Izates’s elder brother Monobazus succeeds him later (20.4.3). Hyman’s printed citation is Bava Batra 11b, while the consulted 11a passage tells of King Monobaz distributing his own and his ancestors’ treasures. Hyman’s explanation connecting the two accounts remains his interpretation.
